unit.title: Emotions and habits
unit.description: Fear, greed, revenge and overtrading: rules so they don't decide for you

steps.title: The market's emotional cycle
steps.body:
Optimism → excitement → **euphoria** (peak risk) → anxiety → denial → fear → **panic and capitulation** (peak opportunity) → despondency → hope → optimism…

Investors tend to buy in euphoria and sell in panic: exactly the opposite of what makes sense.

steps.title: What it looks like in real life
steps.body:
• **Euphoria:** bitcoin in November 2021, on every news bulletin. It then fell by around 75 %.
• **Panic:** March 2020, the S&P 500 drops 34 % in a month because of covid. Within about 5 months it was back at its high.

In both cases, the dominant emotion was pushing people to do the opposite of what worked out.

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: It's not about calling the top or the bottom: nobody does that reliably. It's about not letting fear or greed change a plan written while you were calm.
steps.key: The moment of greatest euphoria is usually the moment of greatest risk; the moment of greatest fear, the greatest opportunity.
steps.tip: When you feel euphoria or panic, don't decide today: reread your plan.

steps.title: What it is
steps.body:
After one or more losses, anger kicks in along with the urge to **win it back now**. So you go in without a signal, double your size or skip your stop.

It's loss aversion at its most expensive: one bad afternoon turns into a bad month.

steps.title: The ready-made rule
steps.body:
**«After 3 losses in a row, I stop for the rest of the day.»**

And also:
• The risk per trade is always the same, whether you win or lose.
• Monthly limit: if you lose 6 % in a month, you stop until the next month.
• You note down in your journal how you were feeling.

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: The market owes you nothing: it doesn't know you've lost. Your next trade has the same odds as if you'd just won.
steps.key: After a loss, the best decision is usually to make no more decisions that day.
steps.tip: After three losses in a row, the best trade is switching off the screen.

steps.title: What the data says
steps.body:
Barber and Odean (2000) studied tens of thousands of US accounts: the 20 % of households that traded most earned **11.4 %** a year versus **17.9 %** for the market.

It's not that they picked worse: every trade pays a commission and the *spread*, and heavy trading usually comes from overconfidence and noise.

steps.title: Noise
steps.body:
The more you watch the market, the more moves you see that mean nothing. And each one seems to demand a decision.

Checking your long-term portfolio every day increases the number of times you see it in the red and the temptation to tinker with it (myopic loss aversion).

steps.title: The cost of overpaying
steps.body: Compare 0.2 % with 1.5 % in annual costs on €10,000 over 30 years at an example 7 %.
steps.tip: Costs compound just like returns, but against you.

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: Fewer trades, better chosen, with low costs. And for the long term: automate your contributions and review your portfolio now and then, not every day.
steps.key: Every trade pays costs: trading a lot turns a small edge into a loss.
steps.tip: In investing, doing nothing is very often the most profitable move.

steps.title: Checklist before every purchase
steps.body:
1. Is it in my plan?
2. Can I explain the reason in three sentences, without saying «because it's going up»?
3. Have I written down three reasons I could be wrong?
4. Do I know where my stop is or what would make me sell?
5. Does the size respect my limits?
6. Am I calm, or am I in a hurry, angry or euphoric?
7. Would I buy it if nobody were talking about it?

If any answer is «no», **don't buy today**.

steps.title: Monthly review
steps.body:
• Have I followed my plan? On which trades not, and why?
• Does my return beat a comparable index?
• Which bias have I spotted in myself this month?

And ask Lumi in Biases mode: Lumi will play devil's advocate.

steps.title: Your takeaway
steps.body: Pilots use checklists even though they know how to fly. Rules written while you're calm decide for you when you're not.
steps.key: You can't get rid of emotions; you can stop them deciding for you.
steps.tip: You don't need to be as cold as a machine. You need rules that work even when you're not.

u28l1-1.prompt: Put this part of the market's emotional cycle in order.
u28l1-1.explanation: Peak risk is in euphoria; peak opportunity, in panic.

u28l1-2.prompt: This is how the S&P 500 was doing during the covid crash. Tap the day of peak panic (the lowest close). (S&P 500 · daily closes · up to 25/03/2020)
u28l1-2.explanation: That March 2020 bottom was the worst time to sell: the index took about 5 months to get back to its high.

u28l1-3.prompt: 25 March 2020: the S&P 500 has just fallen 34 % in a month and the news talks about nothing but panic. What did it do over the following months?
u28l1-3.explanation: Those who sold in the panic locked in the loss and missed the recovery. Fear shouts loudest right near the bottoms.

u28l1-4.prompt: Real chart of a fall. What trend do you see? (Amazon · closes every 3 sessions · December 2025 – February 2026)
u28l1-4.explanation: Lower highs and lower lows: this is fear territory, where most people sell without a plan.

u28l1-5.prompt: March 2020. Your long-term index fund is down 30 % and your group of friends says «this is going to zero». What do you do?
options: Reread my plan and keep up my contributions
Move everything into a single share that «has fallen the most»
Sell everything so I don't lose any more
u28l1-5.explanation: Panic says sell; a plan written while you were calm holds you steady.
feedback: Good: your plan already allowed for falls. Your contributions bought cheap.
Changing plan in the middle of a panic, and concentrating everything, multiplies the risk.
You're selling in the panic: the index was back at its highs within about 5 months and you miss it.

u28l1-6.prompt: November 2021. Everyone's talking about crypto, your friends are bragging about their gains and you feel you're «being left behind». What do you do?
options: Stick to my speculation limit and my plan
Take out a loan to go in big
Put all my savings in before it rises further
u28l1-6.explanation: Euphoria wants more; your written limits say how much at most.
feedback: Good: if anything goes in, it's the small slice you could afford to lose entirely.
Debt at the height of euphoria: the worst possible combination.
That's greed and FOMO right at the peak. Bitcoin fell by around 75 % over the following year.

u28l1-7.prompt: At which stage of the cycle is the risk usually highest?
u28l1-7.explanation: When everyone is in and nobody sees any risks, prices are usually higher than their value justifies.

u28l1-8.prompt: Investors usually buy in panic and sell in euphoria.
u28l1-8.explanation: They usually do exactly the opposite: buy in euphoria and sell in panic.

u28l1-9.prompt: Match each moment in a trade with its typical emotion.
options: The trade is going against you
u28l1-9.explanation: Knowing the emotion of each moment lets you prepare the rule in advance.
right: Anger, the urge to win it back

options: Raising your risk because «I'm on a roll»
Getting into something that's up 200 % so you don't miss out
Removing the stop because «it can't fall any further»
Selling everything after an alarming headline
Closing a small gain out of panic about giving it back
u28l1-10.explanation: Both emotions push you to break your plan, in opposite directions.

u28l2-1.prompt: After several losses, increasing the size of your next trade helps you win it back without extra risk.
u28l2-1.explanation: You're raising your risk just when your decision-making is at its worst. If it goes wrong again, the hole doubles.

u28l2-2.prompt: Ana has lost three trades in a row this morning, all within her plan. She's angry and spots another «opportunity». What does she do?
options: Stops for the rest of the day, notes down how she feels and comes back tomorrow at normal size
Removes her stops so they don't get hit any more
Goes in at triple size to win it all back
u28l2-2.explanation: The 3-loss rule exists for this exact moment.
feedback: Good: three losses is a normal losing streak. What isn't normal is letting anger do the trading.
Without a stop, the next loss has no limit.
That's revenge trading: if it fails, she loses a month's worth in one afternoon.

options: Switch to another asset and carry on
Stop for today: that's revenge trading
u28l2-3.explanation: After a bad run, stopping is a professional decision, not a defeat.
feedback: Switching assets doesn't change the mood you're deciding in.
Ugh, you're right. I'll switch off the screen, note it in my journal and come back tomorrow at 1 %.
The market doesn't know you've lost. Angry and at triple size, you'll most likely lose more.
lines: I've lost 3 times in a row today 😡
Now I'm going all in, the market owes me.

options: Your size doesn't depend on what you lost yesterday: stick to your fixed risk
Good idea, you're on a roll now
u28l2-4.explanation: Forcing yourself to win back losses is the quickest way to make them bigger.
feedback: Leverage only speeds up whatever happens, and haste usually makes it bad.
OK. If my system has an edge, it recovers with time, not with haste.
Making €50 doesn't change the odds of the next trade.
lines: Yesterday I lost €300 and today I've made back €50 😌
If I raise my size, I'll win it all back this afternoon.

u28l2-5.prompt: A €10,000 account. You lose three trades of €100 and, out of anger, risk €600 on the fourth, which you also lose. How much have you lost in total?
u28l2-5.explanation: 3 × 100 + 600 = €900: 9 % of the account in one afternoon. With the stop-for-the-day rule, it would have been €300.

u28l2-6.prompt: Put in order what to do after three losses in a row.
options: Check whether the trades followed the plan
Come back another day at normal size
Note in your journal what happened and how you felt
u28l2-6.explanation: First cut it off, then record, then analyse and, finally, come back without changing your risk.

u28l2-7.prompt: After a loss, your next trade is more likely to work out.
u28l2-7.explanation: That's the gambler's fallacy: each trade is almost independent of the one before.

u28l2-8.prompt: Which signs show you're revenge trading? Select all that apply.
options: You follow your plan with your usual risk
You raise your size to win it back
You go in without your signal being met
u28l2-8.explanation: Following the plan with your usual risk is exactly the opposite.

u28l2-9.prompt: Ready-made rule: after ____ losses in a row, I stop for the rest of the day.
u28l2-9.explanation: It's the textbook rule: it cuts off the spiral before it grows.

u28l2-10.prompt: What do revenge trading and loss aversion have in common?
options: They both make us take on more risk to avoid accepting a loss
u28l2-10.explanation: When we're losing, we become more reckless: «I'll double up to win it back».

u28l3-1.prompt: You make 2 trades a week and each one costs you €6 in commission and spread. How much do you pay in a 52-week year?

u28l3-2.prompt: If your account is €5,000, what annual percentage do those €624 of costs eat up? (round to one decimal place)
u28l3-2.explanation: 624 ÷ 5,000 ≈ 0.125 → 12.5 % a year. You'd have to earn that just to break even.

u28l3-3.prompt: According to Barber and Odean (2000), what annual return did the 20 % of households that traded most get?
u28l3-3.explanation: Trading more cost them over 6 points a year.

u28l3-4.prompt: €10,000 over 30 years at a 7 % return: with 0 % costs you end up with about €76,123; with 1.5 % costs, about €49,840. How much do the costs set you back?
u28l3-4.explanation: 76,123 − 49,840 = €26,283: more than a third of the final result.

u28l3-5.prompt: Bruno makes 20 trades a week because «if I don't trade, I don't win». His journal says that before costs he roughly breaks even and after costs he loses. What should he change?
options: Cut down to the few trades that meet his plan
Switch to a more volatile asset to make more per trade
Trade even more to make up for it
u28l3-5.explanation: If you break even before costs, every extra trade makes you lose.
feedback: Good: fewer trades, better chosen, and costs stop eating up everything.
More volatility doesn't fix a system with no edge: it just makes the losses bigger.
More trades = more costs. The hole gets deeper.

u28l3-6.prompt: The more trades you make, the higher your returns tend to be.
u28l3-6.explanation: Barber and Odean's data says the opposite: those who traded most earned less.

u28l3-7.prompt: Quick: which habit helps you trade less in your long-term portfolio?
options: Automating contributions and reviewing it now and then
u28l3-7.explanation: Fewer triggers, fewer temptations to tinker with it.

options: Buying because a video says «it's going to explode today»
Switching funds every month to whichever rose most
Selling because the portfolio is down 1 % today
Rebalancing once a year according to the plan
u28l3-8.explanation: Useful decisions come from the plan; noise comes from the screen.

u28l3-9.prompt: Match each cost with its description.
u28l3-9.explanation: They all grow with the number of trades.
right: The difference between the buying and selling price
What you pay Hacienda (the Spanish tax authority) on your gains
The daily cost of holding a leveraged position
What the broker charges per trade

options: Careful: more triggers usually lead to more trades and more costs
u28l3-10.explanation: You don't need to see every move: you need to act only when your plan says so.
feedback: That's pure noise.
More alerts usually bring more impulsive trades… and more costs.
You're right. I'll keep alerts only for my stops and targets, and check the rest calmly.
lines: I've set up price alerts on 40 shares 📲
That way I won't miss a thing.

u28l4-1.prompt: Put your anti-bias routine for a trade in order.
options: Every month: review your stats and compare yourself with an index
On exit: note it in your journal
On entry: set your stop and size
During: don't move the stop against you
u28l4-1.explanation: Each moment has its rule: that way emotions can't find a way in.

u28l4-2.prompt: Which questions are on the pre-purchase checklist? Select all that apply.
options: How much has it gone up this week?
Do I know where my stop is?
u28l4-2.explanation: How much it's gone up feeds FOMO, not the decision.

u28l4-3.prompt: Which situations mean «I'm not buying today»? Select all that apply.
options: I've just lost three trades and I'm angry
My plan, my stop and my limits are all met
I don't know where I'd put the stop
I can't explain the reason without saying «because it's going up»
u28l4-3.explanation: If everything checks out and you're calm, the checklist lets you trade.

u28l4-4.prompt: Lumi asks you to go through the checklist. What do you reply?
options: Question 7: would you buy it if nobody were talking about it?
Buy half now and go through the checklist later
u28l4-4.explanation: The checklist only works if you go through it beforehand and in full.
feedback: Hmm… honestly, no. So I'm not buying today.
The checklist comes before buying: afterwards it's no use.
When it's «crystal clear» and you're in a hurry is exactly when you need the checklist most.
lines: I want to buy this share right now 🏃

u28l4-5.prompt: What do you tell her in the monthly review?
options: If you made money, breaking the plan doesn't matter
Review those 4 trades: what made you break it and how did they turn out?
u28l4-5.explanation: The monthly review looks at the process, not just the result.
feedback: Winning while breaking the plan teaches you to break it. One day it'll cost you.
Good idea. Two were FOMO and one was revenge. I'll note them down as my biases of the month.
That's overconfidence after a good month.
lines: But I broke the plan on 4 trades…

u28l4-6.prompt: Match each bias with its antidote.
u28l4-6.explanation: Every bias has a specific rule that keeps it in check.
right: Decide from today, ignoring what's been lost
Track it in your journal and compare yourself with an index

u28l4-7.prompt: Pablo goes through the checklist before buying. Everything is «yes» except number 6: he's euphoric after winning two trades. What does he do?
options: Doesn't buy today and reviews it calmly tomorrow
Buys double because he's on a roll
Buys anyway, 6 out of 7 is pretty good
u28l4-7.explanation: The checklist isn't up for negotiation: a single «no» is enough to wait.
feedback: Good: if the trade still makes sense tomorrow, the checklist will come out 7 out of 7.
Euphoria + bigger size = textbook overconfidence.
The rule says that if any answer is «no», you don't buy today. Number 6 is there for a reason.

u28l4-8.prompt: If you're very experienced, you no longer need a checklist.
u28l4-8.explanation: Pilots use one even though they know how to fly: experience doesn't remove biases.

u28l4-9.prompt: Which monthly review question tells you whether your active management is worth it?
options: How many trades have I made?
Does my return beat a comparable index?
How long have I spent looking at the screen?
u28l4-9.explanation: If you don't beat the index over several years, buying the index would have served you better.

u28l4-10.prompt: If any answer on the checklist is «no», ____ buy today.
u28l4-10.explanation: Waiting a day hardly ever costs you; buying without going through the checklist often does.
